qs.q: If $A_{n\times n}$ is an invertible matrix, then $\det[\operatorname{adj}(A)]=$ ----
e: Since $A$ is invertible, $\det(A)\neq0$, and dividing gives $\det[\operatorname{adj}(A)]=[\det(A)]^{n-1}$.

qs.q: If $A_{2\times2}$ is a matrix such that $\det(A)=3$, then $\det[\operatorname{adj}(A)]=$ ----

e: The adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix: $\operatorname{adj}(A)=\begin{bmatrix}4&-3\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}$.
Shortcut for $2\times2$: swap the diagonal entries and change the sign of the off-diagonal entries. Choice (b) is the cofactor matrix before transposing.

e: $\det(A)\neq0$ is a nonzero scalar and $A^{-1}$ is invertible, so their product is invertible.

qs.q: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&1\\4&8&4\end{bmatrix}$ is an augmented matrix for a linear system, then this system can't be solved by ----
e: Cramer's rule needs a square system whose coefficient matrix has $\det\neq0$.
The coefficient matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\4&8\end{bmatrix}$ with $\det=8-8=0$, so Cramer's rule does not apply.
Gaussian and Gauss-Jordan elimination work for any system: $R_2\to R_2-4R_1$ gives $[0\ 0\ |\ 0]$, so the system has infinitely many solutions.

qs.q: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&2&c\\12&8&d\end{bmatrix}$ is an augmented matrix for a linear system, this system can't be solved by ----
e: Cramer's rule requires $\det\neq0$, so it cannot be used.
Gaussian and Gauss-Jordan elimination can be applied to any system (the result is no solution or infinitely many, depending on $c,d$).
